<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{I}$ be a $\sigma$-ideal on $2^{\omega}$. Define then
        \begin{itemize}
            \item[--] $\mathcal{IA}=\{X\subseteq2^{\omega}:\forall F\in\mathcal{I}$ $X+F\in\mathcal{I}\}$,
            \item[--] $\mathcal{I}^{*}=\{X\subseteq2^{\omega}:\forall F\in\mathcal{I}$ $X+F\neq2^{\omega}\}$
        \end{itemize}
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
(Shelah; \cite{ShelahNAMA})\label{ShelahNAMA}
        A set $X\subseteq2^{\omega}$ is null-additive if and only if for any interval partition $(I_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ there is a slalom $S=(S_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ with $S_{n}\in[2^{I_{n}}]^{n}$ for $n\in\omega$ such that 
        \begin{center}
            $X\subseteq\{x\in2^{\omega}:\forall^\infty n\in\omega$ $x|_{I_{n}}\in S_{n}\}$
        \end{center}
        A set $X\subseteq2^{\omega}$ is meager-additive if and only if for any interval partition $(I_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ there is a real $y\in2^{\omega}$ and an interval partition $(J_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ that dominates $(I_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ such that
        \begin{center}
            $X\subseteq\{x\in2^{\omega}:\forall^\infty n\in\omega$ $\exists k\in\omega$ that $I_{k}\subseteq J_{n}$ and $x|_{I_{k}}= y|_{I_{k}}\}$
        \end{center}
        In particular, $\mathcal{NA}\subseteq\mathcal{MA}$ holds.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
(Zindulka; \cite{ZindulkaMAEA})
        $\mathcal{MA}=\mathcal{EA}$
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
A set $X\subseteq2^{\omega}$ is a \emph{strongly measure zero} set if for every increasing sequence $(f_{n})_{n\in\omega}\in\omega^{\omega}$ there is a sequence $(\sigma_{n})_{n\in\omega}\subseteq 2^{<\omega}$ with $|\sigma_{n}|=f_{n}$ for all $n\in\omega$ and such that 
        \begin{center}
            $X\subseteq\{x\in2^{\omega}:\exists^{\infty}n\in\omega$ $\sigma_{n}\subseteq x\}$
        \end{center}
        The collection of all strongly measure zero sets will be denoted by $\mathcal{SMZ}$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
(Galvin, Mycielski, Solovay; \cite{GalvMycielSolov})
        $\mathcal{SMZ}=\mathcal{M}^{*}$
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{I}\subseteq\mathcal{J}$ will be two arbitrary $\sigma$-ideals on $2^{\omega}$. Define
        \begin{center}
            $\langle\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}\rangle=\{X\subseteq2^{\omega}:\forall F\in\mathcal{I}$ $X+F\in\mathcal{J}\}$,
        \end{center}
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
(Pawlikowski; \cite{PawlikowskiEN})
        $\langle\mathcal{E},\mathcal{N}\rangle=\mathcal{SMZ}$
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
(Recław; see also Bartoszyński, Judah; \cite{BJ})
        $\mathcal{SM}\subseteq\langle\mathcal{E},\mathcal{M}\rangle$
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
The following holds:
        \begin{itemize}
            \item[--] $\langle\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}\rangle\subseteq\mathcal{J}$,
            \item[--] $\mathcal{J}_{0}\subseteq\mathcal{J}_{1}$ implies $\langle\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}_{0}\rangle\subseteq \langle\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}_{1}\rangle$,
            \item[--] $\mathcal{I}_{0}\subseteq\mathcal{I}_{1}$ implies $\langle\mathcal{I}_{1},\mathcal{J}\rangle\subseteq \langle\mathcal{I}_{0},\mathcal{J}\rangle$,
        \end{itemize}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
The following holds:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[--] $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{IA})=\mathrm{add}_{t}(\mathcal{I})$,
        \item[--] $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{I}^{*})=\mathrm{cov}_{t}(\mathcal{I})$,
        \item[--] $\mathrm{non}(\langle\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}\rangle)=\mathrm{add}_{t}(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J})$.
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
(Bartoszyński, Shelah; \cite{BartShClosedMeasureZeroSets})\label{CardInvsofE}
    The following (in)equalities hold:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[--] $\mathrm{add}(\mathcal{E})=\mathrm{add}(\mathcal{M})$ and $\mathrm{cof}(\mathcal{E})=\mathrm{cof}(\mathcal{M})$,
        \item[--] $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{M}),\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{N})\leq\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{E})\leq\max\{\mathfrak{d},\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{N})\}$
        \item[--] $\min\{\mathfrak{b},\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{N})\}\leq\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{E})\leq\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{M}),\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{N})$
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
(Talagrand \cite{Tala} or Theorem 2.2.4. in \cite{BJ})\label{CharacterizationM}
    For an interval partition $I=(I_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ and a real $y\in2^{\omega}$ define the set
    \begin{center}
        $M(y,I)=:\{x\in2^{\omega}:\forall^\infty n\in\omega$ $x|_{I_{n}}\neq y|_{I_{n}}\}$
    \end{center}
    Every set $M(y,I)$ is meager and for every meager set $M\subseteq2^{\omega}$ there are an interval partition $I=(I_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ and a real $y\in2^{\omega}$ such that $M\subseteq M(y,I)$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
(Bartoszyński and Shelah; \cite{BartShClosedMeasureZeroSets})\label{CharacterizationE}
    For an interval partition $I=(I_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ and a slalom $S=(S_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ where $S_{n}\subseteq 2^{I_{n}}$ and $\frac{|S_{n}|}{2^{|I_{n}|}}\leq\frac{1}{2^{n}}$ define the set 
    \begin{center}
        $E(S,I)=:\{x\in2^{\omega}:\forall^\infty n\in\omega$ $x|_{I_{n}}\in S_{n}\}$
    \end{center}
    Every set $E(S,I)$ is an $F_{\sigma}$-set of measure zero and for every $E\in\mathcal{E}$ there are an interval partition $I=(I_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ and a slalom $S=(S_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ such that $E\subseteq E(S,I)$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{X}$ be a collection of subsets of reals. We will write $\mathrm{BC}(\mathcal{X})$, if the class $\mathcal{X}$ consists only of countable sets.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
(Laver; \cite{LaverBorelConj})
    It is consistent that $\mathrm{BC}(\mathcal{SMZ})$ holds.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
(Carlson; \cite{Carlson})\label{CarlsonDualBC}
        It is consistent that $\mathrm{BC}(\mathcal{SM})$.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
(Pawlikowski; \cite{PawlikowskiDualBorel})\label{PawlikowskiDualBC}
If $\mathbb{P}$ is a forcing notion with precaliber equal $\omega_{1}$, then the finite support iteration of length $\omega_{2}$ of $\mathbb{P}$ forces the dual Borel conjecture.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
(Goldstern, Kellner, Shelah, Wohofsky; \cite{BorelWithDualBorel})\label{BorelWithDualBorel}
    It is consistent that $\mathrm{BC}(\mathcal{SMZ})$ and $\mathrm{BC}(\mathcal{SM})$ hold simultaneously.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
(Bartoszyński; \cite{BartoszynskiBD})\label{BartoszynskiMANA}
        \begin{itemize}
            \item[--] $\mathfrak{b}=\omega_{1}$ implies existence of an uncountable meager-additive set,
            \item[--] $\mathfrak{d}=\omega_{1}$ implies existence of an uncountable null-additive set.
        \end{itemize}
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
It is consistent that $\neg \mathrm{BC}(\mathcal{NA})$. In particular, the following constellation of Borel Conjectures holds:
                                    
        \begin{center}
		\begin{tikzpicture}[]
                
			\tikzset{
				textnode/.style={text=black}, 
			}
			\tikzset{
				edge/.style={color=black, thick, opacity=0.8}, 
			}
			\newcommand{2.9}{3.3}
			\newcommand{1.6}{2.0}
			
			\node[textnode] (NA) at (0,  0) {$\mathcal{NA}$};
            \node[textnode] (N) at (0,  1.5*1.6) {$\mathcal{N}^{*}$};
			\node[textnode] (MA) at (2.9,  0) {$\mathcal{MA}$};
			\node[textnode] (EM) at (2.9,  1.5*1.6) {$\langle\mathcal{E},\mathcal{M}\rangle$};
			\node[textnode] (M) at (2.9*2,  0) {$\mathcal{M}^{*}$};
			\node[textnode] (E) at (2.9*2,  1.5*1.6) {$\mathcal{E}^{*}$};
			
			\draw[->, edge] (NA) to (MA);
			\draw[->, edge] (MA) to (EM);
			\draw[->, edge] (MA) to (M);
			\draw[->, edge] (EM) to (E);
            \draw[->, edge] (M) to (E);
            \draw[->, edge] (NA) to (N);
            \draw[->, edge] (N) to (EM);

			\draw[blue,thick] (-0.2*2.9,-0.1*1.6)--(-0.2*2.9,1.6*1.6);

		\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
By Theorem \ref{BartoszynskiMANA}, any model satisfying $\mathfrak{d}=\omega_{1}$ gives the constellation.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{CutInCohenHechler}
        It is consistent that $\mathrm{BC}(\mathcal{N}^{*})$, but $\neg \mathrm{BC}(\mathcal{MA})$. In particular, the following constellation of Borel Conjectures holds:
                                               
        \begin{center}
		\begin{tikzpicture}[]
                
			\tikzset{
				textnode/.style={text=black}, 
			}
			\tikzset{
				edge/.style={color=black, thick, opacity=0.8}, 
			}
			\newcommand{2.9}{3.3}
			\newcommand{1.6}{2.0}
			
			\node[textnode] (NA) at (0,  0) {$\mathcal{NA}$};
            \node[textnode] (N) at (0,  1.5*1.6) {$\mathcal{N}^{*}$};
			\node[textnode] (MA) at (2.9,  0) {$\mathcal{MA}$};
			\node[textnode] (EM) at (2.9,  1.5*1.6) {$\langle\mathcal{E},\mathcal{M}\rangle$};
			\node[textnode] (M) at (2.9*2,  0) {$\mathcal{M}^{*}$};
			\node[textnode] (E) at (2.9*2,  1.5*1.6) {$\mathcal{E}^{*}$};
			
			\draw[->, edge] (NA) to (MA);
			\draw[->, edge] (MA) to (EM);
			\draw[->, edge] (MA) to (M);
			\draw[->, edge] (EM) to (E);
            \draw[->, edge] (M) to (E);
            \draw[->, edge] (NA) to (N);
            \draw[->, edge] (N) to (EM);

			\draw[blue,thick] (0.5*2.9,-0.1*1.6)--(0.5*2.9,1.6*1.6);

		\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
In Cohen and Hechler models, the $\mathcal{N}^{*}$-sets are countable. For Cohen model this follows from Theorem \ref{CarlsonDualBC}, and for Hechler from Theorem \ref{PawlikowskiDualBC}. In Cohen model $\mathfrak{b}=\omega_{1}$, thus by the Theorem \ref{BartoszynskiMANA} there exists uncountable meager-additive sets in that model. In Hechler model $\mathrm{add}(\mathcal{M})=\omega_{2}$, so any set of size $\omega_{1}$ is meager-additive.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
It is consistent that $\mathrm{BC}(\mathcal{SMZ})$, but $\neg \mathrm{BC}(\mathcal{SM})$. In particular, the following constellation of Borel Conjectures holds:
                                                   
        \begin{center}
		\begin{tikzpicture}[]
                
			\tikzset{
				textnode/.style={text=black}, 
			}
			\tikzset{
				edge/.style={color=black, thick, opacity=0.8}, 
			}
			\newcommand{2.9}{3.3}
			\newcommand{1.6}{2.0}
			
			\node[textnode] (NA) at (0,  0) {$\mathcal{NA}$};
            \node[textnode] (N) at (0,  1.5*1.6) {$\mathcal{N}^{*}$};
			\node[textnode] (MA) at (2.9,  0) {$\mathcal{MA}$};
			\node[textnode] (EM) at (2.9,  1.5*1.6) {$\langle\mathcal{E},\mathcal{M}\rangle$};
			\node[textnode] (M) at (2.9*2,  0) {$\mathcal{M}^{*}$};
			\node[textnode] (E) at (2.9*2,  1.5*1.6) {$\mathcal{E}^{*}$};
			
			\draw[->, edge] (NA) to (MA);
			\draw[->, edge] (MA) to (EM);
			\draw[->, edge] (MA) to (M);
			\draw[->, edge] (EM) to (E);
            \draw[->, edge] (M) to (E);
            \draw[->, edge] (NA) to (N);
            \draw[->, edge] (N) to (EM);

			\draw[blue,thick] (-0.1*2.9,0.8*1.6)--(2.1*2.9,0.8*1.6);
            
	\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Judah, Shelah and Woodin showed (\cite{JudShWoodRandomVsBorelConj}) that adding any number of random reals by measure algebra to the model of Borel conjecture preserves Borel conjecture, so let $\mathbb{V}'$ be a model obtained by adding $\omega_{2}$-many random reals to the Laver model of Borel Conjecture. On the one hand, by the Judah, Shelah and Woodin result, $\mathcal{M}^{*}=\mathcal{C}tbl$, on the other, $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{N})=\omega_{2}$ holds in $\mathbb{V}'$, so any set of size $\omega_{1}$ is strongly meager.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
Let $\mathbb{M}$ denote the Miller forcing, i.e. collection of all trees $T\subseteq\omega^{<\omega}$ such that every $\sigma\in T$ can be extended to a $\tau\in T$ such that the set of immediate successors $succ_{T}(\tau)=\{i\in\omega:\tau^{\frown}i\in T\}$ is infinite. The order is inclusion.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
For any uncountable $X\subseteq2^{\omega}$ we have $\mathbb{M}\Vdash"X\notin\mathcal{NA}"$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
According to Shelah characterization of null-additive sets (see Theorem \ref{ShelahNAMA}), we have to show that after adding single Miller real there is an interval partition $I=(I_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ such that for every slalom $(S_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ with $S_{n}\in[2^{I_{n}}]^{n}$ for all $n\in\omega$ there is $x\in X$ such that $x|_{I_{n}}\notin S_{n}$ for infinitely many $n\in\omega$. The desired partition will be the one added by the Miller generic real: if $\dot{r}_{gen}\in\omega^{\omega}$ is the generic real, then $\dot{I}=(\dot{I}_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ is such that $|\dot{I}_{n}|=\dot{r}_{gen}(n)+1$. Now, let $T_{0}\in\mathbb{M}$ be such that 
        \begin{center}
            $T_{0}\Vdash"\dot{S}_{n}=\{\dot{\sigma}^{n}_{1},\dot{\sigma}^{n}_{2},...,\dot{\sigma}^{n}_{n}\}\subseteq 2^{\dot{I}_{n}}$ for every $n\in\omega"$
        \end{center}
        Using standard fusion argument, it is possible to construct a Miller tree $T_{1}\leq T_{0}$ such that for every $\sigma\in split(T_{1})$ and $i\in succ_{T_{1}}(\sigma)$ there is a collection $\{\tau^{(\sigma,i)}_{1},\tau^{(\sigma,i)}_{2},...,\tau^{(\sigma,i)}_{|\sigma|}\}$ such that we have 
        \begin{center}
            $T_{1}|_{\sigma^{\frown}i}\Vdash"\forall k\leq |\sigma|$ $\dot{\sigma}^{|\sigma|}_{k}=\tau^{(\sigma,i)}_{k}"$
        \end{center}
        We need the following claim
        \begin{claim}
            There is $T_{2}\leq T_{1}$ such that for each $\sigma\in split(T_{2})$ there is $\{y^{\sigma}_{k}:k\leq|\sigma|\}\subseteq2^{\omega}$ such that the following condition holds
        \begin{center}
            $\forall N\in\omega$ $\forall^\infty i\in succ_{T_{2}}(\sigma)$ we have $\forall k\leq|\sigma|$ $y^{\sigma}_{k}|_{N}\subseteq \tau^{(\sigma,i)}_{k}$
        \end{center}
        \end{claim}
        \begin{proof}
            We will show how to ensure the required condition on the stem of $T_{1}$. Propagating this construction over all splitnodes by the standard fusion argument produces the requierd tree $T_{2}$.\\
            Let $\sigma^{*}$ be the stem of $T_{1}$. By induction on $k\leq|\sigma^{*}|$ we construct $\{y^{\sigma^{*}}_{k}:k\leq |\sigma^{*}|\}\subseteq2^{\omega}$ and decreasing sequence of trees $T_{1}^{k}\leq T_{1}$, $k\leq|\sigma^{*}|$ as follows: assume that $\{y^{\sigma^{*}}_{l}:l< k\}$ and $T_{1}^{l}$ with $stem(T^{l}_{1})=\sigma^{*}$ have been constructed. We construct $T_{1}^{k}\leq T_{1}^{l}$ with the same stem and $y^{\sigma^{*}}_{k}$ such that for all $N\in\omega$ for almost all $i\in succ_{T^{k}_{1}}(\sigma^{*})$ we have  that $y^{\sigma^{*}}_{k}|_{N}\subseteq \tau^{(\sigma^{*},i)}_{k}$. To do this, find $A_{k}\in [succ_{T^{l}_{1}}(\sigma^{*})]^{\omega}$ such that for some $y\in2^{\omega}$ we have
            \begin{center}
            $\forall N\in\omega$ $\forall^\infty i\in succ_{T^{k}_{1}}(\sigma^{*})$ $y|_{N}\subseteq \tau^{(\sigma^{*},i)}_{k}$
            \end{center}
            Let then $y^{\sigma^{*}}_{k}$ be such $y$ and let $T^{k}_{1}\leq T^{l}_{1}$ be such that $stem(T^{k}_{1})=\sigma^{*}$ and $succ_{T^{k}_{1}}(\sigma^{*})=A_{k}$. This finishes the induction step. When the induction is over, the tree $T^{|\sigma^{*}|}_{1}$ is the required one.
        \end{proof}
        Once the claim is proven, let $x\in X\setminus\{y^{\sigma}_{k}: \sigma\in split(T_{2})$ 
        and $k\leq|\sigma|\}$. We will now construct a tree $T_{3}\leq T_{2}$ such that $T_{3}\Vdash"\exists^{\infty}_{n\in\omega}$ $x|_{\dot{I}_{n}}\notin \dot{S}_{n}"$. For every $\sigma\in split(T_{2})$ let $N_{\sigma}\in\omega$ be such that $y^{\sigma}_{k}|_{N_{\sigma}}\neq x|_{N_{\sigma}}$ for every $k\leq|\sigma|$. Let $T_{3}\leq T_{2}$ be a Miller tree obtained from $T_{2}$ by removing finitely many successors at each splitnode $\sigma$ of $T_{2}$ according to the $N=N_{\sigma}$ in the condition above. This means, that the tree $T_{3}$ has the property that for every $\sigma\in split(T_{3})$ we have
    \begin{center}
        $\forall i\in succ_{T_{3}}(\sigma)$ $T_{3}\Vdash"$ for every $ k\leq |\sigma|$ we have $y^{\sigma}_{k}|_{N_{\sigma}}\subseteq \tau^{(\sigma,i)}_{k}$ and $y^{\sigma}_{k}|_{N_{\sigma}}\neq x|_{N_{\sigma}}"$
    \end{center}
    It follows that
    \begin{center}
        $T_{3}\Vdash"\forall n\in\{m\in\omega:\dot{r}_{gen}|_m\in split(T_{3})\}$ we have $x|_{\dot{I}_{n}}\notin \dot{S}_{n}"$
    \end{center}
    This finishes the proof of the lemma.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- claim-1: body_md -->
There is $T_{2}\leq T_{1}$ such that for each $\sigma\in split(T_{2})$ there is $\{y^{\sigma}_{k}:k\leq|\sigma|\}\subseteq2^{\omega}$ such that the following condition holds
        \begin{center}
            $\forall N\in\omega$ $\forall^\infty i\in succ_{T_{2}}(\sigma)$ we have $\forall k\leq|\sigma|$ $y^{\sigma}_{k}|_{N}\subseteq \tau^{(\sigma,i)}_{k}$
        \end{center}
<!-- end claim-1 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
We will show how to ensure the required condition on the stem of $T_{1}$. Propagating this construction over all splitnodes by the standard fusion argument produces the requierd tree $T_{2}$.\\
            Let $\sigma^{*}$ be the stem of $T_{1}$. By induction on $k\leq|\sigma^{*}|$ we construct $\{y^{\sigma^{*}}_{k}:k\leq |\sigma^{*}|\}\subseteq2^{\omega}$ and decreasing sequence of trees $T_{1}^{k}\leq T_{1}$, $k\leq|\sigma^{*}|$ as follows: assume that $\{y^{\sigma^{*}}_{l}:l< k\}$ and $T_{1}^{l}$ with $stem(T^{l}_{1})=\sigma^{*}$ have been constructed. We construct $T_{1}^{k}\leq T_{1}^{l}$ with the same stem and $y^{\sigma^{*}}_{k}$ such that for all $N\in\omega$ for almost all $i\in succ_{T^{k}_{1}}(\sigma^{*})$ we have  that $y^{\sigma^{*}}_{k}|_{N}\subseteq \tau^{(\sigma^{*},i)}_{k}$. To do this, find $A_{k}\in [succ_{T^{l}_{1}}(\sigma^{*})]^{\omega}$ such that for some $y\in2^{\omega}$ we have
            \begin{center}
            $\forall N\in\omega$ $\forall^\infty i\in succ_{T^{k}_{1}}(\sigma^{*})$ $y|_{N}\subseteq \tau^{(\sigma^{*},i)}_{k}$
            \end{center}
            Let then $y^{\sigma^{*}}_{k}$ be such $y$ and let $T^{k}_{1}\leq T^{l}_{1}$ be such that $stem(T^{k}_{1})=\sigma^{*}$ and $succ_{T^{k}_{1}}(\sigma^{*})=A_{k}$. This finishes the induction step. When the induction is over, the tree $T^{|\sigma^{*}|}_{1}$ is the required one.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
It is consistent that $\mathrm{BC}(\mathcal{NA})$, while $\neg \mathrm{BC}(\mathcal{MA})$ and $\neg \mathrm{BC}(\mathcal{N}^{*})$. In particular, the following constellation of Borel Conjectures holds:
                                               
        \begin{center}
		\begin{tikzpicture}[]
    
			\tikzset{
				textnode/.style={text=black}, 
			}
			\tikzset{

			}

            \node[textnode] (N) at (0,  1.5*1.6) {$\mathcal{N}^{*}$};
			\node[textnode] (MA) at (2.9,  0) {$\mathcal{MA}$};
			\node[textnode] (EM) at (2.9,  1.5*1.6) {$\langle\mathcal{E},\mathcal{M}\rangle$};
			\node[textnode] (M) at (2.9*2,  0) {$\mathcal{M}^{*}$};
			\node[textnode] (E) at (2.9*2,  1.5*1.6) {$\mathcal{E}^{*}$};
			
			\draw[->, edge] (NA) to (MA);
			\draw[->, edge] (MA) to (EM);

			\draw[->, edge] (EM) to (E);
            \draw[->, edge] (M) to (E);

<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Consider a c.s.i. of length $\omega_{2}$ over a model of CH such that random forcing $\mathbb{B}$ and Miller forcing $\mathbb{M}$ alternate as iterands. We claim that in the resulting model $\mathbb{V}^{\omega_{2}}$ the thesis holds. In the final model, on the one hand $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{N})=\omega_{2}$, which means that any set of size $\omega_{1}$ is in $\mathcal{N}^{*}$, on the other, $\mathfrak{b}=\omega_{1}$ so by Bartoszyński Theorem \ref{BartoszynskiMANA} there are uncountable meager-additive sets. We will finish the proof by showing that any null-additive set is countable. Suppose that $X\subseteq2^{\omega}$ is an uncountable set in the final model $\mathbb{V}^{\omega_{2}}$. Without loss of generality, we assume that $X$ is of size $\omega_{1}$. Then there is $\alpha\in\omega_{2}$ such that $X\in\mathbb{V}^{\alpha}$. Then, after adding consecutive Miller real, $X$ is not null-additive. Let $N\in\mathcal{N}\cap \mathbb{V}^{\alpha+1}$ be such that $X+N\notin\mathcal{N}$ holds in $\mathbb{V}^{\alpha+1}$. It follows that the set $X+N$ has positive outer measure. Recall then that both Miller and random forcing (and theirs countable support iterations) preserve outer measure (in \cite{BJ} see Theorem 7.3.47 and Theorem 6.3.13). However, this means that $X+N\notin\mathcal{N}$ holds in $\mathbb{V}^{\omega_{2}}$. This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- theorem-16: body_md -->
\label{NoNAinMillers}
        In Millers model $\mathcal{NA}$-sets are countable while $\mathcal{MA}$-sets are not.
<!-- end theorem-16 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
There are no uncountable strong $\gamma$-sets in Miller model.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- theorem-17: body_md -->
(Calder\'on; \cite{Calderon})\label{CalderonSMZandMA}
        $\mathrm{BC}(\mathcal{SMZ})$ and $\mathrm{BC}(\mathcal{MA})$ are equivalent.
<!-- end theorem-17 -->
<!-- theorem-18: body_md -->
\label{BCofEstarAndEM}
        $\mathrm{BC}(\mathcal{E}^{*})$ and $\mathrm{BC}(\langle\mathcal{E},\mathcal{M}\rangle)$ are equivalent.
<!-- end theorem-18 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
We will only show that $\mathrm{BC}(\mathcal{E}^{*})$ implies $\mathrm{BC}(\langle\mathcal{E},\mathcal{M}\rangle)$. Suppose that $\mathrm{BC}(\mathcal{E}^{*})$ is not true i.e. that there is an uncountable $X\subseteq2^{\omega}$, $X\in\mathcal{E}^{*}$. Without loss of generality, we may assume that $|X|=\omega_{1}$. If $\mathfrak{b}=\omega_{1}$ then by Theorem \ref{BartoszynskiMANA} there is an uncountable meager-additive set, which by  discussion from the introduction is in $\langle\mathcal{E},\mathcal{M}\rangle$. Assume that $\omega_{1}<\mathfrak{b}$. Note that any Borel image of $X$ into $\omega^{\omega}$ is bounded. By the argument similar to the proof of Proposition \ref{NonEMvsNonEstar} (see also Proposition 11 of \cite{Weiss2018}), $X$ is in $\langle\mathcal{E},\mathcal{M}\rangle$, which finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- question-1: body_md -->
Does $\mathrm{BC}(\mathcal{SM})$, $\mathrm{BC}(\langle\mathcal{E},\mathcal{M}\rangle)$ or $\mathrm{BC}(\mathcal{E}^{*})$ hold in Laver model? Is dual Borel conjecture $\mathrm{BC}(\mathcal{N}^{*})$ true in Miller model?
<!-- end question-1 -->
<!-- question-2: body_md -->
Is $\mathrm{BC}(\mathcal{E}^{*})$ (or equivalently $\mathrm{BC}(\langle\mathcal{E},\mathcal{M}\rangle)$) consistent?
<!-- end question-2 -->

<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
A relational system is a triple $\mathcal{R}=\langle\mathcal{X},\preccurlyeq,\mathcal{Y}   \rangle$ where $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$ are non-empty sets and $\preccurlyeq$ is a relation between $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$ i.e. $\preccurlyeq\subseteq\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}$. The bounding and dominating number of a relational system $\mathcal{R}$ is defined as:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[--] $\mathfrak{b}(\mathcal{R})=\min\{|\mathcal{Z}|:\mathcal{Z}\subseteq\mathcal{X}$ $\neg\exists y\in\mathcal{Y}$ $\forall x\in\mathcal{Z}$ $x\preccurlyeq y\}$
        \item[--] $\mathfrak{d}(\mathcal{R})=\min\{|\mathcal{Z}|:\mathcal{Z}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}$ $\forall x\in\mathcal{X}$ $\exists y\in\mathcal{Z}$ $x\preccurlyeq y\}$
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{R}_{0}=\langle\mathcal{X}_{0},\preccurlyeq_{0},\mathcal{Y}_{0}\rangle$ and $\mathcal{R}_{1}=\langle\mathcal{X}_{1},\preccurlyeq_{1},\mathcal{Y}_{1}\rangle$ be two relational systems.
    We will say that a pair of functions $\phi:\mathcal{X}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}_{1}$ and $\psi:\mathcal{Y}_{1}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}_{0}$ forms a Tukey reduction if for any $\mathcal{Z}\subseteq\mathcal{X}_{0}$ and $y\in\mathcal{Y}_{1}$, if $y$ $\preccurlyeq_{1}$-dominates all members of $\phi[\mathcal{Z}]$, then $\psi(y)$ $\preccurlyeq_{0}$-dominates all members of $\mathcal{Z}$. If such pair exists we will say that $\mathcal{R}_{0}$ is Tukey reducible to the $\mathcal{R}_{1}$. If $\mathcal{R}_{0}$ and $\mathcal{R}_{1}$ are Tukey reducible to each other we will say that they are Tukey equivalent.
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
If $\mathcal{R}_{0}$ is Tukey reducible to $\mathcal{R}_{1}$, then 
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[--] $\mathfrak{b}(\mathcal{R}_{1})\leq\mathfrak{b}(\mathcal{R}_{0})$,
        \item[--] $\mathfrak{d}(\mathcal{R}_{0})\leq\mathfrak{d}(\mathcal{R}_{1})$.
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- theorem-19: body_md -->
(Bartoszyński, Fremlin; see \cite{BJ})
    For any increasing $b\in\omega^{\omega}$ we have:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[--] $\mathrm{add}(\mathcal{N})=\mathfrak{b}(\omega^{\omega},\in^{*},\mathcal{S}lm(b))$,
        \item[--] $\mathrm{cof}(\mathcal{N})=\mathfrak{d}(\omega^{\omega},\in^{*},\mathcal{S}lm(b))$.
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end theorem-19 -->
<!-- theorem-20: body_md -->
(Pawlikowski; \cite{PawlikowskiTransitiveInvariants})
        For any increasing $b\in\omega^{\omega}$ we have:
        \begin{itemize}
            \item[-] $\mathrm{add}_{t}(\mathcal{N})=\min\{\mathfrak{b}(\Pi F,\in^{*},\mathcal{S}lm(F,b)):F\in\omega^{\omega}\}$
        \end{itemize}
        In particular $\mathrm{add}(\mathcal{N})=\min\{\mathfrak{b},\mathrm{add}_{t}(\mathcal{N})\}$.
<!-- end theorem-20 -->
<!-- theorem-21: body_md -->
(Cardona, Mejía and Rivera-Madrid; \cite{MejiaCardonaMA})
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[--] $\mathrm{add}(\mathcal{NA})=\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{NA})$
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end theorem-21 -->
<!-- theorem-22: body_md -->
(Carlson; \cite{Carlson}, also \cite{BJ})
    For any increasing $b\in\omega^{\omega}$ we have:
        \begin{itemize}
            \item[-] $\min\{\mathfrak{b}(\Pi F,\in^{*},\mathcal{S}lm(F,b)):F\in\omega^{\omega}\}\leq \mathrm{add}(\mathcal{SMZ})$
        \end{itemize}
<!-- end theorem-22 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
(Kada; \cite{KadaLaverNumber})\label{Kada}
    For any increasing $b\in\omega^{\omega}$ we have:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[--] $\mathrm{cof}(\mathcal{N})=\max\{\mathfrak{d},\sup\{\mathfrak{d}(\Pi F,\in^{*},\mathcal{S}lm(F,b)): F\in\omega^{\omega}\}\}$
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- theorem-23: body_md -->
(Bartoszyński; \cite{BartoszCombAspects}, see also Bartoszyński and Judah\cite{BJ})
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[--] $\mathrm{add}(\mathcal{M})=\mathfrak{b}(\omega^{\omega},\circeq,\omega^{\omega}\times\mathbb{IP})$,
        \item[--] $\mathrm{cof}(\mathcal{M})=\mathfrak{d}(\omega^{\omega},\circeq,\omega^{\omega}\times\mathbb{IP})$.
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end theorem-23 -->
<!-- theorem-24: body_md -->
(Pawlikowski; \cite{PawlikowskiTransitiveInvariants})
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[--] $\mathrm{add}_{t}(\mathcal{M})=\min\{\mathfrak{b}(\Pi F,\circeq,\Pi F\times\mathbb{IP}): F\in\omega^{\omega}\}$
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end theorem-24 -->
<!-- theorem-25: body_md -->
(Cardona, Mejía, Rivera-Madrid; \cite{MejiaCardonaMA})\label{NonCovMAvscovnonHHF}
    The following hold:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[--] $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{MA})=\min\{\mathfrak{b}(\Pi F,\circeq,\Pi F\times\mathbb{IP}):F\in\omega^{\omega}\}$,
        \item[--] $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{MA})\geq\sup\{\mathfrak{d}(\Pi F,\circeq,\Pi F\times\mathbb{IP}):F\in\omega^{\omega}\}$.
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end theorem-25 -->
<!-- theorem-26: body_md -->
(Bartoszyński; \cite{BartoszCombAspects}, Miller; \cite{MillerAddEvsB}, see also \cite{BJ})
For any increasing $b\in\omega^{\omega}$ we have:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[--] $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{M})=\mathfrak{d}(\omega^{\omega},\neq^{*},\omega^{\omega})=\mathfrak{d}(\omega^{\omega},\in^{\infty},\mathcal{S}lm(b))$,
        \item[--] $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{M})=\mathfrak{b}(\omega^{\omega},\neq^{*},\omega^{\omega})=\mathfrak{b}(\omega^{\omega},\in^{\infty},\mathcal{S}lm(b))$.
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end theorem-26 -->
<!-- theorem-27: body_md -->
(Miller; \cite{MillerAddEvsB};  Pawlikowski; \cite{PawlikowskiTransitiveInvariants}; see also \cite{BJ})
        \begin{itemize}
            \item[--] $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{SMZ})=\min\{\mathfrak{d}(\Pi F,\neq^{*},\Pi F): F\in\omega^{\omega}\}=\mathrm{cov}_{t}(\mathcal{M})$
        \end{itemize}
<!-- end theorem-27 -->
<!-- theorem-28: body_md -->
(Miller \cite{MillerAddEvsB})\label{MillerAddMeager}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[--] $\mathrm{add}(\mathcal{M})=\min\{\mathfrak{b}, \min\{\mathfrak{d}(\Pi F,\neq^{*},\Pi F): F\in\omega^{\omega}\}\}$
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end theorem-28 -->
<!-- theorem-29: body_md -->
(Bartoszyński; \cite{BartoszynskiCoveringNull} or Cardona and Mejía; \cite{SlalomNumbersOnReals})\label{covNvsSmallsetInv}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[--] $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{N})\leq\min\{\mathfrak{d}(\Pi F,\in^{\infty},\mathcal{S}lm(F,b)):\Sigma\frac{b(i)}{F(i)}<\infty\}$,
        \item[--] $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{N})\geq\sup\{\mathfrak{b}(\Pi F,\in^{\infty},\mathcal{S}lm(F,b)):\Sigma\frac{b(i)}{F(i)}<\infty\}$
    \end{itemize}
    also
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[--] $\min\{\mathfrak{b},\min\{\mathfrak{d}(\Pi F,\in^{\infty},\mathcal{S}lm(F,b)):\Sigma\frac{b(i)}{F(i)}<\infty\}\}\leq\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{N})$,
        \item[--] $\max\{\mathfrak{d},\sup\{\mathfrak{b}(\Pi F,\in^{\infty},\mathcal{S}lm(F,b)):\Sigma\frac{b(i)}{F(i)}<\infty\}\}\geq\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{N})$
    \end{itemize}
    in particular
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[--] if $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{N})<\mathfrak{b}$, then $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{N})=\mathfrak{d}(\Pi F,\in^{\infty},\mathcal{S}lm(F,b))$ for some $b,F\in\omega^{\omega}$,
        \item[--] if $\mathfrak{d}<\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{N})$, then $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{N})=\mathfrak{b}(\Pi F,\in^{\infty},\mathcal{S}lm(F,b))$ for some $b,F\in\omega^{\omega}$.
    \end{itemize}
    where $\Sigma\frac{b(i)}{F(i)}<\infty$.
<!-- end theorem-29 -->
<!-- theorem-30: body_md -->
(Bartoszyński and Judah; \cite{BartJudahBorelImages})\label{SMestimatesnon}
    The following inequalities hold:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[--] $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{SM})\geq\min\{\mathfrak{d}(\Pi F,\in^{\infty},\mathcal{S}lm(F,b)):\Sigma\frac{b(i)}{F(i)}<\infty\}$,
        \item[--] $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{SM})\leq\min\{\mathfrak{d}(\Pi F,\in^{*},\mathcal{S}lm(F,b)):\Sigma\frac{b(i)}{F(i)}<\infty\}$
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end theorem-30 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{DefinicjaHF}
        Let $F\in\omega^{\omega}$ be an increasing function. Denote by $\mathcal{H}_{F}$ the $\sigma$-ideal on $\Pi F$ generated by the sets of the form
        \begin{center}
            $H_{I,y}=\{x\in\Pi F:\forall^\infty_{n\in\omega}\exists k\in I_{n}$ $x(k)=y(n)\}$
        \end{center}
        where $I=(I_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ is an interval partition and $y\in\Pi F$.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
(Mej\'ia, Cardona, Rivera-Madrid; \cite{MejiaCardonaMA} see also Cardona; \cite{CardonaMA})\label{CardonaBasicIneqNonCovHHF}
    The following inequalities hold for any $F\in\omega^{\omega}$:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[--] $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{M})\leq\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})\leq\mathrm{cof}(\mathcal{M})$
        \item[--] $\mathrm{add}(\mathcal{M})\leq\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})\leq\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{M})$
    \end{enumerate}
    also
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[--] $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})\leq\mathfrak{b}(\Pi F,=^{\infty},\Pi F)$
        \item[--] $\mathfrak{d}(\Pi F,=^{\infty},\Pi F)\leq \mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{addHFbelowB}
    $\mathrm{add}(\mathcal{H}_{F})\leq\mathfrak{b}$ and $\mathfrak{d}\leq\mathrm{cof}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ hold.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
First we show that $\mathrm{add}(\mathcal{H}_{F})\leq\mathfrak{b}$. Let $\{I^{\alpha}:\alpha<\mathfrak{b}\}$ be an unbounded set of interval partitions. For $\alpha<\mathfrak{b}$ and $i\in 2$ define the following set
        \begin{center}
            $X^{i}_{\alpha}=\{x\in\Pi F:\forall n\in\omega$ $x(\max I^{\alpha}_{2n+i})=0\}$.
        \end{center}
        Clearly, every such $X^{i}_{\alpha}$ is in $\mathcal{H}_{F}$. We claim that $\bigcup\{X^{i}_{\alpha}:\alpha<\mathfrak{b}$ and $i\in 2\}\notin\mathcal{H}_{F}$. Assume towards contradiction that for some $y\in\Pi F$ and an interval partition $J=(J_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ we have that
        \begin{center}
            $\bigcup\{X^{i}_{\alpha}:\alpha<\mathfrak{b}$ and $i\in 2\}\subseteq H_{y,J}=\{x\in\Pi F: \forall^\infty n\in\omega$ $\exists k\in J_{n}$ $x(k)=y(k)\}$
        \end{center}
        As the family $\{I^{\alpha}:\alpha<\mathfrak{b}\}$ is unbounded, there is $\alpha<\mathfrak{b}$ such that for infinitely many $n$'s in $\omega$ the interval $J_{n}$ does not contain any $I^{\alpha}_{k}$, $k\in\omega$ and thus is itself contained in two consecutive intervals $I^{\alpha}_{k_{n}}\cup I^{\alpha}_{k_{n+1}}$. Then for some $i\in 2$, for infinitely many $n\in\omega$, $J_{n}\subseteq I^{\alpha}_{k_{n}}\cup I^{\alpha}_{k_{n+1}}$ and the parity of every $k_{n}$ is $i\in2$. Let then $x\in X^{i}_{\alpha}$ be such that $x|_{I^{\alpha}_{k_{n}}\cup I^{\alpha}_{k_{n+1}}}\neq y|_{I^{\alpha}_{k_{n}}\cup I^{\alpha}_{k_{n+1}}}$ for these intervals. But then $x\notin H_{y,J}$, which contradicts the previous assumption.\\
        To see that $\mathfrak{d}\leq\mathrm{cof}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ we dualize the argument above. Let $\kappa<\mathfrak{d}$ and assume that $\{H_{\alpha}:\alpha<\kappa\}\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{F}$. We will show that these sets do not form a basis of $\mathcal{H}_{F}$. Without loss of generality assume that each $H_{\alpha}$ is of form $\{x\in\Pi F:\forall^\infty n\in\omega$ $\exists i\in I^{\alpha}_{n}$ $x(i)=y_{\alpha}(i)\}$ for some $y_{\alpha}\in\Pi F$ and interval partition $I^{\alpha}=(I^{\alpha}_{n})_{n\in\omega}$. As $\kappa<\mathfrak{d}$ there is an interval partition $(J_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ that dominates all $(I^{\alpha}_{n})_{n\in\omega}$'s. Then, similar argument as in the proof of the first inequality shows that the set
        \begin{center}
            $H=\{x\in\Pi F:\forall n\in\omega$ $x(\min J_{n})=0\}$
        \end{center}
        is in $\mathcal{H}_{F}$ and cannot be covered by any $H_{\alpha}$ for $\alpha<\kappa$. This proves the second inequality.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
We have:
        \begin{itemize}
        \item[--] $\mathrm{add}(\mathcal{M})=\min\{\mathrm{add}(\mathcal{H}_{F}):F\in\omega^{\omega}\}$,
        \item[--] $\mathrm{cof}(\mathcal{M})=\max\{\mathrm{cof}(\mathcal{H}_{F}):F\in\omega^{\omega}\}$.
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
If $F\in \omega^{\omega}$ is bounded, then:
        \begin{itemize}
            \item[--] $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})\leq\mathfrak{d}$,
            \item[--] $\mathfrak{b}\leq\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$.
        \end{itemize}
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Assume that $F$ is bounded by $C\in\omega$. To show that $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})\leq\mathfrak{d}$ let $I_{\alpha}=(I_{n}^{\alpha})_{n\in\omega}$'s where $\alpha<\mathfrak{d}$ form a dominating family of interval partitions. We claim that the sets $H_{i,I^{\alpha}}$ for $i\leq C$ and $\alpha<\mathfrak{d}$ cover the entire $\Pi F$. To see this assume that $x\in\ \Pi F$. Let $i\leq C$ and let $J=(J_{n})_{n\in\omega}\in\mathbb{IP}$ be such that for every $n\in\omega$ there is $j\in J_{n}$ with $x(j)=i$. But then, if $\alpha<\mathfrak{d}$ is such that $J\leq^{*}I^{\alpha}$, then $x\in H_{i,I^{\alpha}}$.\\
        To show that $\mathfrak{b}\leq\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ assume that $\kappa<\mathfrak{b}$ and $\{x_{\alpha}:\alpha<\kappa\}\subseteq\Pi F$. For every $\alpha<\kappa$ and $i\leq C$, if there are infinitely many $n\in\omega$ such that $x_{\alpha}(n)=i$, then define an interval partition $I^{i,\alpha}=(I^{i,\alpha}_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ such that for every $n\in\omega$ there is $j\in I^{i,\alpha}_{n}$ such that $x_{\alpha}(j)=i$. Let $J$ be an interval partition that dominated all $I^{i,\alpha}$'s, $i\leq C$, $\alpha<\kappa$. Then clearly $\{x_{\alpha}:\alpha<\kappa\}\subseteq\bigcup_{i\leq C}H_{i,J}$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
For any increasing $F\in\omega^{\omega}$ the following inequalities are consistent:
        \begin{itemize}
            \item[--] $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})<\mathfrak{b}$,
            \item[--] $\mathfrak{d}<\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$,
            \item[--] $\mathfrak{b}<\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$,
            \item[--] $\mathfrak{d}<\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ for $F\in\omega^{\omega}$ such that $\Sigma_{n}\frac{1}{F(n)}<\infty$,
            \item[--] $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})<\mathfrak{b}$.
        \end{itemize}
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
First, we show the consistency of $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})<\mathfrak{b}$. The inequality holds in Laver model in which $\mathfrak{b}=\mathfrak{d}=\omega_{2}$. To show that $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})=\omega_{1}$ in Laver model we will use the following claim and the fact that Laver forcing (and its countable support iteration) has the Laver property.
        \begin{claim}\label{claimLaverProperty1}
            For an increasing $F\in\omega^{\omega}$ Laver property keeps $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ small.
        \end{claim}
        \begin{proof}
            Let $p\Vdash"\dot{y}\in\Pi F$ and $\dot{I}=(\dot{I}_{n})_{n}\in\mathbb{IP}"$. Let $q\leq p$ and $S=(S_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ be such that $q\Vdash"\forall^\infty n\in\omega$ $\dot{y}(n)\in S_{n}"$. Without loss of generality, we may assume that $|S_{n}|< F(n)$ for every $n\in\omega$. Then any $x\in\Pi F$ such that $x(n)\in F(n)\setminus S_{n}$ satisfies $q\Vdash"x\notin H_{\dot{y}, \dot{I}}"$.
        \end{proof}
        As the Laver property keeps $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ small and is preserved by countable support iteration, the $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})=\omega_{1}$ holds in the Lavers model.\\
        
        Next, we show the consistency of $\mathfrak{d}<\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$. Fix an interval partition $I=(I_{n})_{n\in\omega}$. We say that $A\subseteq \Pi_{i\in I_{n}}F(i)$ is good if $A=\{\tau\in \Pi_{i\in I_{n}}F(i):\exists i\in I_{n}$ $\tau(i)=\sigma(i)\}$ for some $\sigma\in \Pi_{i\in I_{n}}F(i)$. Let $Good_{n}$ stands for the collection of good subsets of $\Pi_{i\in I_{n}}F(i)$. Define the forcing $\mathbb{P}$ as follows: $T\in \mathbb{P}$ if
            \begin{enumerate}
                \item[1.] $T$ is a finitely splitting tree,
                \item[2.] for every $t\in T$ and $n\in dom(t)$ $t(n)\subseteq  \Pi_{i\in I_{n}}F(i)$ is good,
                \item[3.] $lim_{t\in T} norm_{n}(succ_{T}(t))=\infty$
            \end{enumerate}
            where the norm $norm_{n}:\mathcal{P}(Good_{n})\rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ is recursively defined as follows: for $\mathcal{A}\subseteq Good_{n}$
            \begin{enumerate}
                \item[\textbf{a)}] $norm_{n}(\mathcal{A})\geq 0$ if and only if $\bigcup\mathcal{A}=\Pi_{i\in I_{n}}F(i)$,
                \item[\textbf{b)}] if $norm_{n}(\mathcal{A})=l+1$ and $\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}_{0}\cup\mathcal{A}_{1}$ then $norm_{n}(\mathcal{A}_{0})\geq l$ or $norm_{n}(\mathcal{A}_{1})\geq l$.
            \end{enumerate}
            In particular $\textbf{a)}$ and $\textbf{b)}$ implies that
            \begin{enumerate}
                \item[\textbf{c)}] if $norm_{n}(\mathcal{A})=l+1$ and $\sigma\in \Pi_{i\in I_{n}}F(i)$ then $norm_{n}(\{A\in\mathcal{A}:\sigma\in A\})\geq l$
            \end{enumerate}
            Clearly if $G\subseteq\mathbb{P}$ is generic filter then $\dot{R}_{gen}=\bigcup\bigcap G$ is a function with domain $\omega$ and for every $n\in\omega$ $\dot{R}_{gen}(n)\in Good_{n}$. In particular, there is $\dot{r}_{gen}\in \Pi F$ such that for every $n\in\omega$ we have
            \begin{center}
                $\dot{R}_{gen}(n)=\{\tau\in \Pi_{i\in I_{n}}F(i):\exists i\in I_{n}$ $\tau(i)=(\dot{r}_{gen}|_{I_{n}})(i)\}$
            \end{center}
            Standard density argument together with the property $\textbf{c)}$ shows that for every $x\in \Pi F$ from the ground model we have $x\in H_{I,r_{gen}}$. It follows that in $\mathbb{V}^{\omega_{2}}$ (the model obtained by countable support iteration of $\mathbb{P}$ of length $\omega_{2}$ over a model of $GCH$) we have $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})=\omega_{2}$.\\
            We will show that the forcing $\mathbb{P}$ is $\omega^{\omega}$-bounding and thus $\mathfrak{d}=\omega_{1}$ holds in $\mathbb{V}^{\omega_{2}}$.\\
            For $T\in\mathbb{P}$ and $n\in\omega$ define
            \begin{center}
                $lvl_{n}(T)=\min\{m\in\omega:\forall t\in T$ ($|t|\geq m \rightarrow norm(succ_{T}(t))\geq n$)$\}$
            \end{center}
            and let $T\leq_{n}S$ if $T\leq S$ and $\{t\in T:|t|\leq lvl_{n}(S)\}=\{t\in S:|t|\leq lvl_{n}(S)\}$. We will now show that the forcing notion $\mathbb{P}$ is $\omega^{\omega}$-bounding. Similar argument shows that it has axiom A.\\
            We will need the following claim
            \begin{claim}
                $\forall T\Vdash"\dot{a}\in\omega"$ $\forall n\in\omega$ $\exists S\leq_{n} T$ $\exists X\subseteq\omega$ finite such that $S\Vdash"\dot{a}\in X"$.
            \end{claim}
            \begin{proof}
            Define the rank function $rank:T\rightarrow\omega$ such that for $t\in T$ we have: 
                \begin{center}
                    $rank(t)=0$ iff there is $n$-tree with stem $t$ which decides the value of $\dot{a}$,\\
                    $rank(t)=l+1$ iff $norm(\{A\in succ_{T}(t): rank(t^{\frown}A)=l\})\geq norm(succ_{T}(t))-1$
                \end{center}
                First, notice that the rank is well-defined for all $t\in T$. This is because if for some $t\in T$ the rank would be undefined $rank(t)=\infty$ then $norm(\{A\in succ_{T}(t):rank(t^{\frown}A)$ is defined$\})<norm(succ_{T}(t))-1$ and thus by the condition $\textbf{b)}$ we have $norm(\{A\in succ_{T}(t):rank(t^{\frown}A)$ is not defined$\})\geq norm(succ_{T}(t))-1$. Using this we can inductively construct a tree $S\in \mathbb{P}$, $S\leq T$ with stem $t$ such that for every $s\in S$ that extends the stem the $rank(s)$ is not defined. But then no extension of $S$ can decide the value of $\dot{a}$.\\
                For every $t\in T$ of length $lvl_{n}(T)$ we will construct the a tree $S_{t}\leq T|_{t}$ such that
                \begin{enumerate}
                    \item[--] $stem(S_{t})=t$,
                    \item[--] $\forall s\in S_{t}$ ( $t\subseteq s$ $\rightarrow$ $norm_{n}(succ_{S_{t}}(s))\geq n$)
                    \item[--] $S_{t}$ forces $\dot{a}$ into a finite set
                \end{enumerate}
                If $t$ is of rank $0$, then such tree exists by the definition. If $rank(t)>0$, then there is a finite tree $R\subseteq T|_{t}$ such that 
                \begin{itemize}
                    \item[--] $\forall s\in term(R)$ $rank(s)=0$,
                    \item[--] $\forall s\in R\setminus term(R)$ that extends $t$, $norm(succ_{R}(s))\geq norm(succ_{T}(s))-1$
                \end{itemize}
                Then let $S_{t}\leq T|_{t}$ be such that $R\subseteq S_{t}$ and for every $s\in term(R)$ $S_{t}|_{s}$ decides the value of $\dot{a}$. Then the tree $S:=\bigcup\{S_{t}:t\in T$ and $|t|=lvl_{n}(T)\}$ forces $\dot{a}$ into a finite set and also $S\leq_{n}T$.
            \end{proof}
            Assume now that $T\Vdash"\dot{f}\in\omega^{\omega}"$. Using the claim above we can inductively construct a sequence $\{T_{n}:n\in\omega\}\subseteq \mathbb{P}$ and a sequence $\{X_{n}:n\in\omega\}$ of finite subsets of $\omega$ such that $T_{0}=T$ and for every $n\in\omega$ we have $T_{n+1}\leq_{n}T_{n}$ and $T_{n+1}\Vdash"\dot{f}(n)\in X_{n}"$. Clearly, if $S$ is fusion of the sequence $\{T_{n}:n\in\omega\}$, then $S$ forces that $\dot{f}$ is dominated by a ground model function.\\

        Next, we show the consistency of $\mathfrak{b}<\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$. The inequality holds in the model obtained by c.s.i. of length $\omega_{2}$ with $\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{H}_{F}}=\mathcal{B}or(\Pi F)\setminus\mathcal{H}_{F}$ as each iterand. In this model we have $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})=\omega_{2}$ as we add appropriate generic reals along the iteration. On the other hand, by Theorem \ref{ZapletalClosedSetsForcingProperties} $\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{H}_{F}}$ preserves Baire category (see also \cite{Cieslak}) so $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{M})=\omega_{1}$ in the iterated model.\\

        Next, we show the consistency of $\mathfrak{d}<\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ for $F\in\omega^{\omega}$ fast enough that $\Sigma_{n}\frac{1}{F(n)}<\infty$. This inequality holds in random model. It is well-known that $\mathfrak{d}=\omega_{1}<\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{N})=\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{E})=\mathfrak{c}=\omega_{2}$ holds in that model. On the other hand, by Proposition \ref{CardonaMAnons} we have that $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{E})\leq\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ for $F\in\omega^{\omega}$ such that $\Sigma_{n}\frac{1}{F(n)}<\infty$.\\

        Next, we show the consistency of $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})<\mathfrak{b}$. To show this, we again use Laver model in which $\mathfrak{b}=\omega_{2}$. To complete the proof, we will show the following simple observation.
        \begin{claim}\label{claimLaverProperty2}
            For an increasing $F\in\omega^{\omega}$ Laver property keeps $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ small.
        \end{claim}
        \begin{proof}
            Assume that  $p\Vdash"\dot{x}\in\Pi F"$ and let $I=(I_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ be such interval partition that $|I_{n}|=n+1$ for all $n\in\omega$. Let $q\leq p$ and $S=(S_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ be such that
            \begin{itemize}
                \item[--] $\forall n\in\omega$ $\forall \sigma\in S_{n}$ $\sigma:I_{n}\rightarrow\omega$ is below $F$,
                \item[--] $q\Vdash"\forall^\infty n\in\omega$ $\dot{x}|_{I_{n}}\in S_{n}"$.
            \end{itemize}
            Let then $y\in\Pi F$ be such that for all $n\in\omega$ and every $\sigma\in S_{n}$ there is unique $i\in I_{n}$ such that $y(i)=\sigma(i)$. Such $y$ exists as $|S_{n}|=|I_{n}|$. Then, clearly $q\Vdash"\dot{x}\in H_{y, I}"$.
        \end{proof}
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- claim-2: body_md -->
\label{claimLaverProperty1}
            For an increasing $F\in\omega^{\omega}$ Laver property keeps $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ small.
<!-- end claim-2 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Let $p\Vdash"\dot{y}\in\Pi F$ and $\dot{I}=(\dot{I}_{n})_{n}\in\mathbb{IP}"$. Let $q\leq p$ and $S=(S_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ be such that $q\Vdash"\forall^\infty n\in\omega$ $\dot{y}(n)\in S_{n}"$. Without loss of generality, we may assume that $|S_{n}|< F(n)$ for every $n\in\omega$. Then any $x\in\Pi F$ such that $x(n)\in F(n)\setminus S_{n}$ satisfies $q\Vdash"x\notin H_{\dot{y}, \dot{I}}"$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->

$\forall T\Vdash"\dot{a}\in\omega"$ $\forall n\in\omega$ $\exists S\leq_{n} T$ $\exists X\subseteq\omega$ finite such that $S\Vdash"\dot{a}\in X"$.
<!-- end claim-3 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Define the rank function $rank:T\rightarrow\omega$ such that for $t\in T$ we have:

<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- claim-4: body_md -->
\label{claimLaverProperty2}
            For an increasing $F\in\omega^{\omega}$ Laver property keeps $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ small.

<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Assume that  $p\Vdash"\dot{x}\in\Pi F"$ and let $I=(I_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ be such interval partition that $|I_{n}|=n+1$ for all $n\in\omega$. Let $q\leq p$ and $S=(S_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ be such that
            \begin{itemize}
                \item[--] $\forall n\in\omega$ $\forall \sigma\in S_{n}$ $\sigma:I_{n}\rightarrow\omega$ is below $F$,
                \item[--] $q\Vdash"\forall^\infty n\in\omega$ $\dot{x}|_{I_{n}}\in S_{n}"$.
            \end{itemize}
            Let then $y\in\Pi F$ be such that for all $n\in\omega$ and every $\sigma\in S_{n}$ there is unique $i\in I_{n}$ such that $y(i)=\sigma(i)$. Such $y$ exists as $|S_{n}|=|I_{n}|$. Then, clearly $q\Vdash"\dot{x}\in H_{y, I}"$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{HHFvsSplittingReaping}
        For any increasing $F\in\omega^{\omega}$ the following inequalities are consistent:
        \begin{itemize}
            \item[--] $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})<\mathfrak{s}$,
            \item[--] $\mathfrak{s}<\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$,
            \item[--] $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})<\mathfrak{r}$,
            \item[--] $\mathfrak{r}<\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$,
            \item[--] $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})<\mathfrak{s}$,
            \item[--] $\mathfrak{s}<\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$,
            \item[--] $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})<\mathfrak{r}$,
            \item[--] $\mathfrak{r}<\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ for sufficiently fast $F$.
        \end{itemize}
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
First, we show the consistency of $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})<\mathfrak{s}$. The inequality holds in iterated Mathias model. It is well-known that Mathias forcing add an unsplit real and thus forces $\mathfrak{s}=\omega_{2}=\mathfrak{c}$ in the final model. To see that $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ remains small we use Claim \ref{claimLaverProperty1} and the fact that Mathias forcing (and its countable support iterations) has the Laver property.\\

    Next, we show the consistency of $\mathfrak{s}<\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$. The inequality follows from the consistency of $\mathfrak{s}<\mathrm{add}(\mathcal{M})$ (which holds for example in Hechler model) and the fact that $\mathrm{add}(\mathcal{M})\leq\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ (by Proposition \ref{CardonaBasicIneqNonCovHHF}).\\

    Next, we show the consistency of$\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})<\mathfrak{r}$. The inequality again holds in Mathias model in which $\mathfrak{r}=\omega_{2}$ as Mathias forcing adds splitting reals. Also follows from the consistency of $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})<\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{E})$ (see Proposition \ref{HHFvsClosedNull}) and the inequality $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{E})\leq\mathfrak{r}$.\\
        
    Next, we show the consistency of $\mathfrak{r}<\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$. The inequality follows from the consistency of $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{M})<\mathfrak{r}$ (which holds, for example, in Silver model) and the inequality $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})\leq\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{M})$ (by Proposition \ref{CardonaBasicIneqNonCovHHF}).\\

    Next, we show the consistency of $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})<\mathfrak{s}$. The inequality holds in Mathias model as Mathias forcing adds unsplit real and has the Laver property (see Claim \ref{claimLaverProperty2}).\\

    Next, we show the consistency of $\mathfrak{s}<\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$. The inequality follows from the consistency of $\mathfrak{s}<\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{M})$ (which holds, for example, in Cohen model) and the inequality $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{M})<\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ (by Proposition \ref{CardonaBasicIneqNonCovHHF}). Also follows from the consistency of $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{E})<\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ (see Proposition \ref{HHFvsClosedNull}) and the inequality $\mathfrak{s}\leq\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{E})$.\\
        
    Next, we show the consistency of $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})<\mathfrak{r}$. The inequality follows from the consistency of $\mathrm{cof}(\mathcal{M})<\mathfrak{r}$ (which holds for example in Silver model or Splitting tree model) and $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})\leq\mathrm{cof}(\mathcal{M})$ (by Proposition \ref{CardonaBasicIneqNonCovHHF}) which holds in particular in Silver model.\\

    Next, we show the consistency of $\mathfrak{r}<\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ for sufficiently fast $F$. In \cite{Zapl1} Zapletal has shown that the forcing notion $\mathbb{PT}_{F,g}$ (see \cite{BJ} Definition 7.3.3. for the definition of the $\mathbb{PT}_{F,g}$) keeps $\mathfrak{r}$ small if $F$ is sufficiently fast (we skip the technical condition of what it precisely means). On the other hand this forcing add an $F$-eventually different real and thus increases $\mathfrak{b}(\Pi F,\neq^{*},\Pi F)$. It follows that in the iterated $\mathbb{PT}_{F,g}$-model we have the inequality $\mathfrak{r}<\mathfrak{b}(\Pi F,\neq^{*},\Pi F)$ holds. As we have $\mathfrak{b}(\Pi F,\neq^{*},\Pi F)\leq\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ (by Proposition \ref{CardonaBasicIneqNonCovHHF}) the inequality $\mathfrak{r}<\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ follows.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
(Mej\'ia, Cardona, Rivera-Madrid; \cite{MejiaCardonaMA}, or Cardona;\cite{CardonaMA})\label{CardonaMAnons}
        For any $F\in\omega^{\omega}$ we have the following:
        \begin{itemize}
            \item[--] if $\Sigma_{i}\frac{1}{F(i)}<\infty$, then $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})\leq\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{E})$ and $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{E})\leq\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$,
            \item[--] if $\Sigma_{i}\frac{1}{F(i)}=\infty$, then $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{N})\leq\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ and $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})\leq\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{N})$.
        \end{itemize}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{HHFvsClosedNull}
        The following equalities are consistent for increasing $F\in\omega^{\omega}$:
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item[--] $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})<\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{E})$ for $F\in\omega^{\omega}$ such that $\Sigma_{i}\frac{1}{F(i)}=\infty$,
            \item[--] $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{E})<\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ for sufficiently fast $F$,
            \item[--] $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})<\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{E})$,
            \item[--] $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{E})<\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$,
            \item[--] $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})<\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{E})$,
            \item[--] $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{E})<\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$,
            \item[--] $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})<\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{E})$,
            \item[--] $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{E})<\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ for $F\in\omega^{\omega}$ such that $\Sigma_{i}\frac{1}{F(i)}=\infty$.
        \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
First, we show the consistency of $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})<\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{E})$ for $F\in\omega^{\omega}$ such that $\Sigma_{i}\frac{1}{F(i)}=\infty$. The inequality follows from the consistency of $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{N})<\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{N})$ (which holds in the random model) and the inequalities $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})\leq\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{N})$ (by Lemma \ref{CardonaMAnons}) and $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{N})\leq\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{E})$.\\
        
    Next, we show the consistency of $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{E})<\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ for sufficiently fast $F$. This follows from the consistency of $\mathfrak{r}<\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ (see Proposition \ref{HHFvsSplittingReaping}) and the inequality $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{E})\leq\mathfrak{r}$. Also follows from the consistency of $\max\{\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{N}),\mathfrak{d}\}<\mathfrak{d}(\Pi F,=^{\infty},\Pi F)$ and the inequalities $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{E})\leq\max\{\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{N}),\mathfrak{d}\}$ (by Theorem \ref{CardInvsofE}) and $\mathfrak{d}(\Pi F,=^{\infty},\Pi F)\leq\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ (by Proposition \ref{CardonaBasicIneqNonCovHHF}).\\
        
    Next, we show the consistency of $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})<\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{E})$. The inequality follows from the consistency of $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})<\mathfrak{s}$ (see Proposition \ref{HHFvsSplittingReaping}) and the inequality $\mathfrak{s}\leq\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{E})$.\\
        
    Next, we show the consistency of $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{E})<\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$. The inequality holds in the model obtained by c.s.i. of length $\omega_{2}$ with $\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{H}_{F}}=\mathcal{B}or(\Pi F)\setminus\mathcal{H}_{F}$ as each iterand. In this model, we have $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})=\omega_{2}$ as we add appropriate generic reals along the iteration. On the other hand, by Theorem \ref{ZapletalClosedSetsForcingProperties} $\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{H}_{F}}$ preserves Baire category (see also \cite{Cieslak}) so $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{E})\leq\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{M})=\omega_{1}$ in the iterated model.\\
        
    Next, we show the consistency of $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})<\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{E})$. The inequality holds in the model obtained by c.s.i. of length $\omega_{2}$ with $\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{E}}=\mathcal{B}or(2^{\omega})\setminus\mathcal{E}$ as each iterand. As in the previous inequality, from the fact that $\mathcal{E}$ is generated by closed sets, we get that in the model we have $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})\leq\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{M})=\omega_{1}$.\\
    
    Next, we show the consistency of $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{E})<\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$. The inequality follows from the consistency of $\mathfrak{r}<\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ (by Proposition \ref{HHFvsSplittingReaping}) and the inequality $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{E})\leq\mathfrak{r}$.\\
    
    Next, we show the consistency of $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})<\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{E})$. The inequality follows from the consistency of $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})<\mathfrak{s}$ (by Proposition \ref{HHFvsSplittingReaping}) and the inequality $\mathfrak{s}\leq\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{E})$.\\
        
    Next, we show the consistency of $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{E})<\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ for $F\in\omega^{\omega}$ such that $\Sigma_{i}\frac{1}{F(i)}=\infty$. This follows from the consistency of $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{N})<\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{N})$ (which holds in the random model) and the inequalities $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{N})\leq\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$ (by Lemma \ref{CardonaMAnons}) and $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{E})\leq\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{N})$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The inequalities 
        \begin{center}
            $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})\leq\mathfrak{d}(\Pi F,=^{\infty},\Pi F)$ and $\mathfrak{b}(\Pi F,=^{\infty},\Pi F)\leq\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})$
        \end{center}
         are not provable in ZFC. On the one hand $\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{H}_{F})\geq\mathrm{add}(\mathcal{M})$ holds in ZFC and on the other $\mathfrak{d}(\Pi F,=^{\infty},\Pi F)<\mathrm{add}(\mathcal{M})$ holds in Hechler model (see \cite{BrendleLoweEventDiff}). Dually, the inequality $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{H}_{F})\leq\mathrm{cof}(\mathcal{M})<\mathfrak{b}(\Pi F,=^{\infty},\Pi F)$ holds in the dual Hechler model.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
(Zapletal; \cite{Zapl1})
    Let $\mathcal{J}$ be a $\sigma$-ideal on a Polish space. Define then the idealized forcing notion $\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{J}}=(\mathrm{Borel}\setminus\mathcal{J},\subseteq)$ consisting of $\mathcal{J}$-positive Borel sets, such that $B\leq C$ means $B\subseteq C$.
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- theorem-31: body_md -->
(Zapletal; \cite{Zapl1})\label{ZapletalClosedSetsForcingProperties}
    If $\mathcal{J}$ is generated by closed sets, then forcing $\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{J}}$ is proper, has continuous reading of names and preserves Baire category.
<!-- end theorem-31 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{NoTreeForHF}
    Compact subsets of $\Pi F$ are not dense in the forcing $\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{H}_{F}}$.
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Let $G=\{y\in\Pi F:\exists^{\infty}_{n}y(n)=0\}$. We will show that $G$ is $\mathcal{H}_{F}$-positive but any closed subset of $G$ is in $\mathcal{H}_{F}$. To see the former fix a set $H_{x,f}$. Without loss of generality we may assume that each interval $[f(n),f(n+1))$ consists of at least two elements. To see that $G\setminus H_{x,f}\neq\emptyset$ let $y\in\Pi F$ be such that for every $n\in\omega$, $y(i_{n})=x(i_{n})$ for some $i_{n}\in[f(n),f(n+1))$ and $y(i_{n}+1)=0$. Then $y\in G\setminus H_{x,f}$.\\
        To see the latter let $D\subseteq G$ be closed and let $D=[T]$ for some pruned tree $T\subseteq Seq(F)$. As $D$ is compact, there are $A_{n}\subseteq T$ such that for every $n\in\omega$:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $A_{n}$ is a finite maximal antichain in $(T,\subseteq)$,
        \item $\max\{|\tau|:\tau\in A_{n}\}+1<\min\{|\tau|:\tau\in A_{n+1}\}$,
        \item for every $\tau\in A_{n}$ we have $\tau(|\tau|-1)=0$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Let now $f\in\omega^{\omega}$ be such that $f(n)=\max\{|\tau|:\tau\in A_{n}\}$. We claim that $D\subseteq H_{x,f}$ where $x\in\Pi F$ is the constant sequence with the value $0$. Clearly, if $x\in[T]$ then there is an increasing sequence $(k_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ such that $x|_{k_{n}}\in A_{n}$ so $x(k_{n}-1)=0$ and $k_{n}\in[f(n),f(n+1))$, which means that $x\in H_{x,f}$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
In the iterated $\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{H}_{F}}$-model (countable support iteration of $\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{H}_{F}}$ of length $\omega_{2}$ over a model of CH) we have $\mathfrak{d}=\omega_{2}$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- question-4: body_md -->
\label{DoesPHFpreservesPpoints}
    Investigate the following properties of $\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{H}_{F}}$:
        \begin{itemize}
            \item[--] Is there a condition $B\in\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{H}_{F}}$ such that $\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{H}_{F}}|_{B}$ is $\omega^{\omega}$-bounding? What about the condition $B=\{x\in\Pi F:\forall i\in\omega$ $\forall^\infty n\in\omega$ $x(n)\neq i\}$?
            \item[--] Does $\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{H}_{F}}$ preserve measure for a function $F\in\omega^{\omega}$ such that $\Sigma_{i}\frac{1}{F(i)}<\infty$?
            \item[--] Does $\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{H}_{F}}$ add splitting reals?
            \item[--] Does $\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{H}_{F}}$ preserves P-points?
            \item[--] Is $\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{H}_{F}}$ homogeneous? 
            \item[--] Does $\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{H}_{F}}$ add Cohen reals? 
        \end{itemize}
<!-- end question-4 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{NonEMvsNonEstar}
    The following inequality holds:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[--] $\min\{\mathfrak{b},\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{E}^{*})\}\leq\mathrm{non}(\langle\mathcal{E},\mathcal{M}\rangle)\leq\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{E}^{*})$
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
The inequality $\mathrm{non}(\langle\mathcal{E},\mathcal{M}\rangle)\leq\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{E}^{*})$ follows from the inculsion $\langle\mathcal{E},\mathcal{M}\rangle\subseteq\mathcal{E}^{*}$. To show that $\min\{\mathfrak{b},\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{E}^{*})\}\leq\mathrm{non}(\langle\mathcal{E},\mathcal{M}\rangle)$, assume $\kappa<\min\{\mathfrak{b},\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{E}^{*})\}$. Let $X=\{x_{\alpha}:\alpha<\kappa\}\subseteq2^{\omega}$ and $E\in\mathcal{E}$. We want to show that $X+E$ is meager. Enumerate $2^{<\omega}$ as $\{\sigma_{n}:n\in\omega\}$. As $\kappa<\mathrm{non}(\mathcal{E}^{*})$, for every $n\in\omega$ there is $x_{n}\in[\sigma_{n}]\setminus\bigcup_{\alpha<\kappa}(E+x_{\alpha})$. For each $\alpha<\kappa$ let $f_{\alpha}\in\omega^{\omega}$ be such that for every $n\in\omega$ we have $[x_{n}|_{f_{\alpha}(n)}]\cap (E+x_{\alpha})=\emptyset$. As $\kappa<\mathfrak{b}$, there is $g\in\omega^{\omega}$ that dominates all $f_{\alpha}$'s. Clearly then
        \begin{center}
            $\bigcup_{\alpha<\kappa}(E+x_{\alpha})\subseteq2^{\omega}\setminus\bigcup_{n\in\omega}[x_{n}|_{g(n)}]$
        \end{center}
        and the latter is a meager set. This finishes the proof of the first inequality.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{LemmaTranslatinalE}
        There is $E\in\mathcal{E}$ such that for every $Y\subseteq2^{\omega}$, if $E+Y\in\mathcal{E}$, then for some $y\in2^{\omega}$ we have that $Y\subseteq E+y$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
In this proof we are going to use the following notation: if $R\subseteq2^{<\omega}$ it a finite tree, by $[R]$ we will denote the union of basic open sets given by the terminal nodes of $R$, i.e. $[R]=\bigcup\{[\sigma]:\sigma$ is a terminal node of $R\}$.\\
           
           Let $g\in\omega^{\omega}$ be defined as $g(n)=n\cdot2^{n^{2}}$ and let $f\in\omega^{\omega}$ as  $f(0)=0$ and $f(n+1)= f(n)+n+g(n)\cdot 2^{f(n)}$ for each $n\in\omega$. We start with the following claim
           \begin{claim}\label{claimWithConditions}
               For every $n\in\omega$ there is 
               \begin{itemize}
                   \item[--] a set $B_{n}\subseteq2^{[f(n),f(n+1))}$,
                   \item[--] and a collection $\{A_{s}\subseteq2^{[f(n),f(n+1))}:s\in2^{f(n)}\}$
               \end{itemize}
                such that for every $n\in\omega$ the following conditions hold:
               \begin{itemize}
               \setlength\itemsep{0.4em}
                   \item[(a)] $\frac{|A_{s}|}{2^{f(n+1)-f(n)}}= \frac{1}{2^{n}}(1-\frac{1}{2^{g(n)}})$,
                   \item[(b)] $\frac{|B_{n}|}{2^{f(n+1)-f(n)}}= \frac{1}{2^{n}}(1-(1-\frac{1}{2^{2^{f(n)}}})^{g(n)})$,
                   \item[(c)] for all $s, t\in2^{f(n)}$ and $\sigma,\tau\in 2^{[f(n),f(n+1)-n)}$, if $s\neq t$ then the sets\\ $A_{s}|_{[f(n),f(n+1)-n)}+\sigma$, and $A_{t}|_{[f(n),f(n+1)-n)}+\tau$ are probabilistically independent,
                   \item[(d)] for every $ Y\subseteq2^{[f(n),f(n+1))}$, if $|Y|\leq g(n)$, then $Y+(2^{[f(n),f(n+1))}\setminus B_{n})\neq 2^{[f(n),f(n+1))}$.
               \end{itemize}
           \end{claim}
           \begin{proof}
               Split the interval $[f(n),f(n+1))$ into $(g(n)+1)$-many intervals $J_{k}$, $k\leq g(n)$ where $|J_{g(n)}|=n$ and for $k<g(n)$, $|J_{k}|=2^{f(n)}$ i.e. $J_{k}=\{j^{k}_{s}:s\in 2^{f(n)}\}$. Define now 
               \begin{center}
                   $A_{s}=\{\sigma\in 2^{[f(n),f(n+1))}:\sigma|_{J_{g(n)}}\equiv0$ and $\exists k<g(n)$ $\sigma(j^{k}_{s})=0\}$,\\
                   $B_{n}=\{\sigma\in 2^{[f(n),f(n+1))}:\sigma|_{J_{g(n)}}\equiv0$ and $\exists k<g(n)$ $\sigma|_{J_{k}}\equiv 0\}$
               \end{center}
               Clearly $B_{n}\subseteq A_{s}$ for every $s\in 2^{f(n)}$. Points $(a)$ and $(b)$ are standard calculations and are similar. Therefore we deal only with the second one:
               \begin{center}
                    $\vspace{8px}\frac{|B_{n}|}{2^{f(n+1)-f(n)}}=\frac{|\{\sigma\in2^{[f(n),f(n+1)-n)}:\textbf{ }\exists k<g(n)\textbf{ }\sigma|_{J_{k}}\equiv0\}|}{2^{f(n+1)-f(n)}}=\newline\vspace{8px}=\frac{2^{f(n+1)-f(n)-n}-|\{\sigma\in2^{[f(n),f(n+1)-n)}:\textbf{ }\forall k<g(n)\textbf{ }\sigma|_{J_{n}}\neq0\}|}{2^{f(n+1)-f(n)}}=\frac{2^{f(n+1)-f(n)-n}-\Pi_{k<g(n)}(2^{2^{f(n)}-1})}{2^{f(n+1)-f(n)}}=\frac{1}{2^{n}}[1-(1-\frac{1}{2^{2^{f(n)}}})^{g(n)}]$
               \end{center}          
               We check the last condition. Let $Y=\{\sigma_{k}:k<g(n)\}$ and define
               \begin{center}
                    $\sigma^{*}=\sigma_{0}|_{J_{0}}$$^{\frown}...^{\frown}\sigma_{g(n)-1}|_{J_{g(n)-1}}$$^{\frown}0^{n}\in 2^{[f(n),f(n+1))}$
               \end{center}
               We claim that $\sigma^{*}\notin Y+(2^{[f(n),f(n+1))}\setminus B_{n})$. This is because, if $\sigma^{*}=\sigma_{k}+\tau$, where $k<g(n)$ and $\tau\notin B_{n}$, then for every $k<g(n)$ there is $i_{k}\in J_{k}$ such that $\tau(i_{k})=1$. This gives the contradicton, as $\sigma^{*}(i_{k})=\sigma_{k}(i_{k})+\tau(i_{k})=\sigma^{*}(i_{k})+1$. This finishes the proof of the claim.
           \end{proof}
           Define now the sets
           \begin{center}
               $E=\{x\in 2^{\omega}:\forall^\infty n\in\omega$ $x|_{[f(n),f(n+1))}\in A_{x|_{f(n)}}\}$,\\
               $F=\{x\in2^{\omega}:\forall^\infty n\in\omega$ $x|_{[f(n),f(n+1))}\in B_{n}\}$.
           \end{center}
           As $B_{n}\subseteq A_{s}$, we have that $F\subseteq E$, and both $E$ and $F$ are $F_{\sigma}$'s of measure zero because of points (a) and (b). We claim that the set $E$ is the one we are looking for, while the set $F$ will have auxiliary role. Suppose that $Y\subseteq 2^{\omega}$ is such that $E+Y\in \mathcal{E}$.
           \begin{claim}
               There is a slalom $S=(S_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ such that for every $n\in\omega$ we have:
               \begin{itemize}
                   \item[--] $S_{n}\subseteq2^{[f(n),f(n+1))}$,
                   \item[--] $|S_{n}|\leq g(n)$
                   \item[--] $Y\subseteq\{x\in2^{\omega}:\forall^\infty n\in\omega$ $x|_{[f(n),f(n+1))}\in S_{n}\}$
               \end{itemize}
           \end{claim}
           \begin{proof}
               Let $R\subseteq2^{<\omega}$ be a tree such that $[R]=\{x\in2^{\omega}:\forall n\in\omega\textbf{ }x|_{[f(n),f(n+1))}\in A_{x|_{f(n)}}\}$. It follows that $[R]+Y\in\mathcal{E}$. Let $\{T_{m}:m\in\omega\}$ be such collection of trees on $2^{<\omega}$ that $[R]+Y\subseteq\bigcup_{n}[T_{m}]$ and every $[T_{m}]$ is of measure zero. By Baire category theorem we have that 
               \begin{center}
                   $\forall y\in Y$ $\exists\sigma\in R$ $\exists m\in\omega$ $[R|_{\sigma}]+y\subseteq[T_{m}]$
               \end{center}
            Thus, if $Y_{\sigma,m}=\{y\in Y:[R|_{\sigma}]+y\subseteq[T_{m}]\}$, then $Y=\bigcup_{\sigma,m}Y_{\sigma,m}$. To construct the required slalom $S=(S_{n})_{n\in\omega}$, for every $\sigma$ and $m$ we will first construct a slalom $S^{\sigma,m}=(S_{n}^{\sigma,m})_{n\in\omega}$ with $S_{n}^{\sigma,m}\subseteq2^{[f(n),f(n+1))}$ and $|S_{n}^{\sigma,m}|\leq 2^{n^{2}}$ such that
            \begin{center}
                $Y_{\sigma,m}\subseteq\{x\in2^{\omega}:\forall^\infty n\in\omega $ $y|_{[f(n),f(n+1))}\in S_{n}^{\sigma,m}\}$
            \end{center}
            When these slaloms are constructed, we define $S=(S_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ as a diagonal union over $S^{\sigma,m}$'s as follows: enumerate all pairs $(\sigma,m)\in R\times \omega$ as $\{(\sigma_{k},m_{k}):k\in\omega\}$ and then for every $n\in\omega$ define $S_{n}=\bigcup_{k\leq n}S^{\sigma_{k},m_{k}}_{n}$. Then, we clearly have that $|S_{n}|\leq n\cdot 2^{n^{2}}=g(n)$ and also $Y\subseteq\{x\in2^{\omega}:\forall^\infty n\in\omega$ $x|_{[f(n),f(n+1))}\in S_{n}\}$ This will finish the proof of the claim.\\
            To construct the slalom $S^{\sigma,m}$ fix $\sigma$ and $m$. For every $n\in\omega$ define
            \begin{center}
                $S_{n}^{\sigma,m}=\{y|_{[f(n),f(n+1))}:y\in Y_{\sigma,m}\}$
            \end{center}
            We only have to check that $|S_{n}^{\sigma,m}|\leq 2^{n^{2}}$. Let $\widetilde{S}_{n}^{\sigma,m}=\{y|_{f(n+1)}:y\in Y_{\sigma,m}\}$. As $|S_{n}^{\sigma,m}|\leq|\widetilde{S}_{n}^{\sigma,m}|$ we will only have to estimate the size of $\widetilde{S}_{n}^{\sigma,m}$. Let $N\in\omega$ be large enough so that $\frac{|T_{m}\cap 2^{n}|}{2^{n}}<\frac{1}{2}$ for every $n>N$. Then for such $n$'s we have that:
            \begin{center}
                $\bigcup_{y\in Y_{\sigma,m}}(R\cap 2^{f(n+1)})+y|_{f(n+1)}=\bigcup_{\tau\in \widetilde{S}_{n}^{\sigma,m}}(R\cap 2^{f(n+1)})+\tau\subseteq T_{m}\cap 2^{f(n+1)}$
            \end{center}
            Thus we have that:
            \begin{center}
                $\vspace{8px}\frac{1}{2}\geq\mu(\bigcup_{y\in Y_{\sigma,m}}R\cap 2^{f(n+1)}+y|_{f(n+1)})=1-\mu(\bigcap_{\tau\in\widetilde{S}_{n}^{\sigma,m}}2^{\omega}\setminus[R\cap2^{f(n+1)}+\tau])\geq\newline \vspace{8px}\geq 1-\Pi_{\tau\in\widetilde{S}_{n}^{\sigma,m}}\mu(2^{\omega}\setminus[R\cap2^{f(n)}+\tau])=1-\Pi_{\tau\in\widetilde{S}_{n}^{\sigma,m}}[1-\mu([R\cap2^{f(n+1)}]+\tau)]=\newline=1-\Pi_{\tau\in\widetilde{S}_{n}^{\sigma,m}}[1-\frac{|R\cap2^{f(n+1)}|}{2^{f(n+1)}}]=1-[1-\Pi_{i=0}^{n}\frac{|A_{s_{i}}|}{2^{f(i+1)-f(i)}}]^{|\widetilde{S}_{n}^{\sigma,m}|}=1-[1-\Pi_{i=0}^{n}\frac{1}{2_{i}}(1-\frac{1}{2^{g_{i}}})]^{|\widetilde{S}_{n}^{\sigma,m}|}$
            \end{center}
            and then
            \begin{center}
                $\vspace{8px}\frac{1}{2}\leq(1-\Pi_{i=0}^{n}\frac{1}{2_{i}}(1-\frac{1}{2^{g_{i}}}))^{|\widetilde{S}_{n}^{\sigma,m}|}\leq(1-\Pi_{i=0}^{n}\frac{1}{2_{i}}(1-\frac{1}{2}))^{|\widetilde{S}_{n}^{\sigma,m}|}=\newline =[1-\frac{1}{2^{\Sigma_{i=0}^{n}(i+1)}}]^{|\widetilde{S}_{n}^{\sigma,m}|}\leq(1-\frac{1}{2^{n^{2}}})^{|\widetilde{S}_{n}^{\sigma,m}|}$
            \end{center}
            It follows that
            \begin{center} $|\widetilde{S}_{n}^{\sigma,m}|\leq2^{n^{2}}$
            \end{center}





               
           \end{proof}
           Now we will make use of the set $F$. We have the following claim.
           \begin{claim}
               $Y+(2^{\omega}\setminus F)\neq 2^{\omega}$
           \end{claim}
           \begin{proof}
               According to the last item of the claim \ref{claimWithConditions}, for every $n\in\omega$, there is $\sigma^{*}_{n}\in 2^{[f(n),f(n+1))}$ such that $\sigma^{*}_{n}\notin S_{n}+(2^{[f(n),f(n+1))}\setminus B_{n})$. Define then $z=\sigma^{*}_{n}$$^{\frown}\sigma^{*}_{n}$$^{\frown}...$ in $2^{\omega}$. We claim that $z\notin Y+(2^{\omega}\setminus F)$. Suppose towards a contradiction that $z=y+x$ where $y\in Y$ and $x\notin F$. Then there is $n\in\omega$ such that $y|_{[f(n),f(n+1))}\in S_{n}$ and $x|_{[f(n),f(n+1))}\notin B_{n}$. This contradicts the fact that $(y+x)|_{[f(n),f(n+1))}=z|_{[f(n),f(n+1))}=\sigma^{*}_{n}\notin S_{n}+(2^{[f(n),f(n+1))}\setminus B_{n})$.
           \end{proof}
           Once the last claim is proven, the rest of the lemma easily follows. Let $z\notin Y+(2^{\omega}\setminus F)$. Then clearly we have $z+Y\subseteq F\subseteq E$ which finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- claim-5: body_md -->
\label{claimWithConditions}
               For every $n\in\omega$ there is 
               \begin{itemize}
                   \item[--] a set $B_{n}\subseteq2^{[f(n),f(n+1))}$,
                   \item[--] and a collection $\{A_{s}\subseteq2^{[f(n),f(n+1))}:s\in2^{f(n)}\}$
               \end{itemize}
                such that for every $n\in\omega$ the following conditions hold:
               \begin{itemize}
               \setlength\itemsep{0.4em}
                   \item[(a)] $\frac{|A_{s}|}{2^{f(n+1)-f(n)}}= \frac{1}{2^{n}}(1-\frac{1}{2^{g(n)}})$,
                   \item[(b)] $\frac{|B_{n}|}{2^{f(n+1)-f(n)}}= \frac{1}{2^{n}}(1-(1-\frac{1}{2^{2^{f(n)}}})^{g(n)})$,
                   \item[(c)] for all $s, t\in2^{f(n)}$ and $\sigma,\tau\in 2^{[f(n),f(n+1)-n)}$, if $s\neq t$ then the sets\\ $A_{s}|_{[f(n),f(n+1)-n)}+\sigma$, and $A_{t}|_{[f(n),f(n+1)-n)}+\tau$ are probabilistically independent,
                   \item[(d)] for every $ Y\subseteq2^{[f(n),f(n+1))}$, if $|Y|\leq g(n)$, then $Y+(2^{[f(n),f(n+1))}\setminus B_{n})\neq 2^{[f(n),f(n+1))}$.
               \end{itemize}
<!-- end claim-5 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Split the interval $[f(n),f(n+1))$ into $(g(n)+1)$-many intervals $J_{k}$, $k\leq g(n)$ where $|J_{g(n)}|=n$ and for $k<g(n)$, $|J_{k}|=2^{f(n)}$ i.e. $J_{k}=\{j^{k}_{s}:s\in 2^{f(n)}\}$. Define now

                   $A_{s}=\{\sigma\in 2^{[f(n),f(n+1))}:\sigma|_{J_{g(n)}}\equiv0$ and $\exists k<g(n)$ $\sigma(j^{k}_{s})=0\}$,\\

               \end{center}
               Clearly $B_{n}\subseteq A_{s}$ for every $s\in 2^{f(n)}$. Points $(a)$ and $(b)$ are standard calculations and are similar. Therefore we deal only with the second one:

                    $\vspace{8px}\frac{|B_{n}|}{2^{f(n+1)-f(n)}}=\frac{|\{\sigma\in2^{[f(n),f(n+1)-n)}:\textbf{ }\exists k<g(n)\textbf{ }\sigma|_{J_{k}}\equiv0\}|}{2^{f(n+1)-f(n)}}=\newline\vspace{8px}=\frac{2^{f(n+1)-f(n)-n}-|\{\sigma\in2^{[f(n),f(n+1)-n)}:\textbf{ }\forall k<g(n)\textbf{ }\sigma|_{J_{n}}\neq0\}|}{2^{f(n+1)-f(n)}}=\frac{2^{f(n+1)-f(n)-n}-\Pi_{k<g(n)}(2^{2^{f(n)}-1})}{2^{f(n+1)-f(n)}}=\frac{1}{2^{n}}[1-(1-\frac{1}{2^{2^{f(n)}}})^{g(n)}]$
               \end{center}          
               We check the last condition. Let $Y=\{\sigma_{k}:k<g(n)\}$ and define
               \begin{center}
                    $\sigma^{*}=\sigma_{0}|_{J_{0}}$$^{\frown}...^{\frown}\sigma_{g(n)-1}|_{J_{g(n)-1}}$$^{\frown}0^{n}\in 2^{[f(n),f(n+1))}$
               \end{center}
               We claim that $\sigma^{*}\notin Y+(2^{[f(n),f(n+1))}\setminus B_{n})$. This is because, if $\sigma^{*}=\sigma_{k}+\tau$, where $k<g(n)$ and $\tau\notin B_{n}$, then for every $k<g(n)$ there is $i_{k}\in J_{k}$ such that $\tau(i_{k})=1$. This gives the contradicton, as $\sigma^{*}(i_{k})=\sigma_{k}(i_{k})+\tau(i_{k})=\sigma^{*}(i_{k})+1$. This finishes the proof of the claim.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- claim-6: body_md -->
There is a slalom $S=(S_{n})_{n\in\omega}$ such that for every $n\in\omega$ we have:
               \begin{itemize}
                   \item[--] $S_{n}\subseteq2^{[f(n),f(n+1))}$,
                   \item[--] $|S_{n}|\leq g(n)$
                   \item[--] $Y\subseteq\{x\in2^{\omega}:\forall^\infty n\in\omega$ $x|_{[f(n),f(n+1))}\in S_{n}\}$
               \end{itemize}
